persona: Apply the perspective of a data/build-pipeline engineer who has shipped generate-then-commit corpora consumed by a strict downstream parser — someone fluent in the failure modes where a lenient generator (skip + warn) and a strict consumer (panic-on-invalid) silently diverge, where a 'count' assertion is gamed by data shape (aliases, duplicates) rather than validated content, and where a --check staleness guard is only as good as what actually invokes it in the gate chain.
review_areas: Trace the panic-on-invalid (Rust loader) vs skip+warn (Python generator) mismatch to its conclusion: a malformed data/issues/*.yaml file is silently SKIPPED by the generator (stderr WARN only, not a build failure), producing a valid-looking committed JSON with fewer entries — could a corpus regression land committed, pass --check (which only compares against what the generator itself would currently produce), and go unnoticed because the 353-count assertion just re-derives the same already-reduced number rather than checking against the real corpus size?

Verify the alias-handling logic against the '353 distinct' claim end-to-end: aliases are inserted into the same IssueRegistry HashMap as primary ids, so confirm the corrected test (HashSet-of-issue_id count per Task 2 Step 2's NOTE) is what actually gets wired in — is there a concrete risk an executor ships the ORIGINAL Step-1 assertion (issue_registry().len() == 353) verbatim, since the NOTE lives as prose after a complete code block rather than as the code block itself?

Confirm the pillar-map's 'covers all 16 labels or the loader panics' guarantee is airtight in practice, not just in theory: since the panic fires lazily on first access to issue_registry() (via OnceLock), and include_str! is a compile-time string embed with no content validation, could a broken corpus/map pairing pass --check (which never invokes the Rust loader) and pass cargo build (panic is runtime, not compile-time), only exploding later — and is every one of the 16 labels actually exercised by the two named unit tests, or could a rare label be reachable in the 353-entry corpus but untested?

Assess the generated-JSON staleness guard's blind spot: gen_issue_registry.py --check exists but check whether any task's verify block, the referee (Task 7), or the orchestrator's final gate (Task 9) actually RUNS --check as part of the gate chain — if not, could a stale committed issue_registry.json (out of sync with data/issues/*.yaml, e.g. after an unrelated corpus edit lands) ship silently, since include_str! only requires the committed file to parse, not to be current?

Evaluate the routing table's content correctness (Infrastructure->tainter_complexity, Technology->compute, Human Capital->[labor,demographics], Rival Orgs->intelligence, Health->demographics) for downstream mis-routing risk, and check whether 'approximate: true' actually surfaces anywhere a human or eval process would see it — note that IssueBoardRow (Task 3) drops nearest_type even though IssueRegistryEntry computes it, and confirm whether that's an intentional Phase-2 trim or a silent information loss worth flagging.

Check the generator's YAML-shape assumptions against what the real 353 data/issues/*.yaml files actually contain: does list(doc['affectedSystems']) tolerate a single-string value instead of a list, does the '_'-prefix skip rule miss a real authored file, and is the '353' figure in the plan's prose actually verified against the live corpus or merely asserted?
